mainTopic: The differences between דיני ממונות and דיני נפשות (including שור הנסקל), who may serve as a judge, and how the סנהדרין was arranged.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about רב's rule: it applies to students like רב כהנא and רב אסי. Next, רבי אבהו teaches that an ox judged for stoning (שור הנסקל) gets none of the special capital-case rules except a court of twenty-three. רב אחא בר פפא learns this from the פסוק 'do not tilt the judgment of your poor.' The גמרא then checks the count of ten differences, finds only nine in the משנה, and supplies a tenth from a ברייתא: judges who may lack mercy are not seated on the סנהדרין. For a מסית the reverse applies. The גמרא then explains that 'all are fit' to judge money cases includes both a גר and a ממזר, and why both had to be taught. Next it finds sources for why capital-case judges need a clean family line and a whole body. Finally a new משנה describes the סנהדרין sitting in a half circle with scribes recording the judges' opinions.

steps.title: Which students רב's rule is talking about
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב's rule refers to students like רב כהנא and רב אסי, who needed רב's traditions but not his reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב said his rule, he meant students like רב כהנא and רב אסי, who needed רב's traditions but did not need רב's reasoning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an earlier problem by narrowing who רב's rule is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule does not cover every kind of student. It is about students like רב כהנא and רב אסי. They still needed the traditions they received from רב, but they could work out the reasoning on their own. Defining the group this way removes the earlier contradiction.

phrases.english: When Rav said [his rule],
[he meant students] such as Rav Kahana and Rav Asi,
who needed Rav's traditions,
but did not need Rav's reasoning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves a difficulty raised before this section by limiting the scope of רב's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule (אוקימתא of who it applies to)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's rule seemed to apply to every student.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב's rule is about students like רב כהנא and רב אסי.

steps.title: The ten differences do not apply to an ox that is to be stoned
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו teaches that none of the ten differences between money cases and capital cases apply to שור הנסקל, except for the need for twenty-three judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: There are ten differences between money cases and capital cases, and none of them apply to an ox that is to be stoned, except for twenty-three judges.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי אבהו says that an ox judged for stoning follows money-case rules, with one exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our פרק's משנה listed ways that capital cases differ from money cases. An ox that killed a person is judged for its life, so you might expect the capital-case rules to apply. רבי אבהו says only one of them carries over: the court of twenty-three.

keyTerms.meaning: an ox that is to be stoned (for killing a person)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
There are ten things [that differ]
between monetary cases and capital cases,
and none of them apply to an ox that is to be stoned,
except for [the need for] twenty-three [judges].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Of the ten differences between דיני ממונות and דיני נפשות, only the court of twenty-three applies to שור הנסקל.
steps.confusionAlert: The ox is still judged by a court of twenty-three, like a capital case. Only the other procedures, which are there to help the accused, are not used for it.

steps.title: Asking for the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי אבהו's rule comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רבי אבהו's rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ox is judged for its life, treating it like a money case needs a basis. The גמרא wants a פסוק that shows the capital-case protections do not apply to it.

keyTerms.meaning: from where do we know these things?

phrases.english: From where are these matters [derived]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source showing the capital-case protections do not apply to שור הנסקל.

steps.title: The source: do not tilt the judgment of your poor
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר פפא learns from the פסוק that you may not tilt the judgment of 'your poor', but you may tilt the judgment of an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר פפא said: The פסוק says, 'Do not tilt the judgment of your poor in his case.' You may not tilt the judgment of your poor, but you may tilt the judgment of an ox that is to be stoned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק that shows the ox does not get the protections a person gets.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The capital-case rules tilt the trial toward finding the accused not guilty. The פסוק says not to tilt the judgment of 'your poor', a person. רב אחא בר פפא reads this to mean the ox does not get those protections.

keyTerms.meaning: do not tilt / do not bend
the judgment of your poor person

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the capital-case procedures exist to protect a human being on trial.

phrases.english: Rav Aha bar Pappa said:
As the verse states:
"You shall not tilt the judgment of your poor in his case."
The judgment of your poor you may not tilt,
but you may tilt
the judgment of an ox that is to be stoned.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר פָּפָּא: דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'לא תטה משפט אביונך' limits the protection to people. An ox's judgment may be tilted.

steps.title: Ten? There are only nine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו's count: the differences add up to nine, not ten.
steps.simpleTranslation: Ten? There are only nine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the number 'ten' in רבי אבהו's statement. It says the list only has nine differences.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you count the differences between money cases and capital cases, you get nine. So the number ten looks wrong.

phrases.english: Ten?
But there are only nine!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the number in רבי אבהו's statement from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The number 'ten' in רבי אבהו's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counting the differences gives only nine.

steps.title: But the משנה itself lists ten
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the משנה clearly teaches ten differences.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches ten!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last step. The משנה itself lists ten items, so how can we say there are only nine?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the claim of 'nine' is the thing under question. The listed items do add up to ten. This sets up the explanation in the next step.

phrases.english: But [the משנה] teaches ten!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the claim of step 5 that there are only nine.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that there are only nine differences.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה itself lists ten items.

steps.title: Two items in the list count as one
steps.stepSummary: The list looks like ten, but 'not everyone is fit' and 'twenty-three judges' are really one rule, so there are nine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because 'not everyone is fit' and 'twenty-three' are one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the objection still stands: two items in the משנה's list are really a single rule, so the משנה only has nine differences. The next step answers how רבי אבהו can still say ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists 'not everyone is fit to judge capital cases' and 'capital cases need twenty-three judges' as two items. These belong together as one rule, so the real count is nine. This also matters for רבי אבהו's rule: the one exception he named, the court of twenty-three, is that combined item.

keyTerms.meaning: not everyone is fit (to judge capital cases)

steps.whatToRemember: An ox judged for stoning gets only one capital-case rule, a court of twenty-three. In the משנה's list, 'not everyone is fit' and 'twenty-three' count as one item, so the משנה gives nine differences. The next step finds a tenth.

phrases.english: Because [the rule that] not all are fit [to judge capital cases]
and [the rule of] twenty-three – are one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 by defending step 5's count of nine; step 8 then restores the count to ten.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Merging two listed items into one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's list seemed to have ten separate differences.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Not all are fit' and 'twenty-three' are one rule, so there are nine differences.

steps.title: The tenth difference: no judges who may lack mercy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supplies a tenth difference from a ברייתא: a very old person, a castrated person, or someone without children is not seated on the סנהדרין. רבי יהודה adds a cruel person.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is another difference. A ברייתא teaches: we do not seat on the סנהדרין an old person, a castrated person, or someone with no children. רבי יהודה adds: also a cruel person.
steps.whatsHappening: In step 7 the count dropped to nine. Now the גמרא finds a tenth difference so that רבי אבהו's count of ten works again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These people may lack the soft heart that comes from raising young children. A capital case needs judges who will look for ways to save the accused, so they are left off the סנהדרין. This rule does not apply to money cases, so it counts as the tenth difference.

phrases.english: But there is another one,
phrases.notes: Another difference between capital and money cases. This one brings the count back up to ten.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא:
We do not seat on the Sanhedrin
an old person or a castrated person
or one who has no children.
Rabbi Yehuda adds:
even a cruel person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills the gap left by step 7, which reduced the count to nine.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Supplies a missing item from an outside source (a ברייתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: After joining two items into one, only nine differences seemed left.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seating only merciful judges on the סנהדרין is the tenth difference, so רבי אבהו's count stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The ten differences are complete: nine from the משנה plus the rule from the ברייתא that judges in capital cases must be people likely to have mercy.

steps.title: The opposite rule for one who entices to idolatry
steps.stepSummary: For a מסית, the opposite applies: the תורה says not to pity him, so the merciful-judge rule does not work in his favor.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the opposite of these applies to a מסית, as the Merciful One says: 'You shall not pity, and you shall not cover up for him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a side comment: in the case of a מסית, the usual push toward mercy is reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא kept judges who might lack mercy off the סנהדרין. With a מסית it is the reverse: the פסוק forbids pity, so those same judges may sit on his case.

keyTerms.meaning: one who entices others to worship idols

phrases.english: And the opposite of these applies to one who entices to idolatry,
as the Merciful One said:
"You shall not pity, and you shall not cover up for him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side note on step 8's mercy rule, showing the one case where it is reversed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a מסית, the court does not lean toward mercy, because the פסוק forbids pitying him.

steps.title: What does 'all' come to include?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה, 'all are fit to judge דיני ממונות', and asks what the word 'all' adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'All are fit to judge money cases.' What does 'all' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a line of the משנה and asks what extra person the word 'all' is meant to include.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'all' seems to stretch the rule to someone we might have thought could not judge. The גמרא wants to know who that is.

phrases.english: All are fit
to judge money cases.
"All" comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the ten differences to a new line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which person is included by the word 'all' in the משנה.

steps.title: רב יהודה: it includes a ממזר
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that 'all' comes to include a ממזר as fit to judge money cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: it comes to include a ממזר.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question: the word 'all' teaches that even a ממזר may judge money cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ממזר has a lineage problem, so we might think he cannot judge. The extra word 'all' tells us he may judge money cases.

keyTerms.meaning: a child born from a forbidden relationship (such as adultery or incest)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
To include a mamzer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'all' includes a ממזר as fit to judge money cases.

steps.title: But we already learned this in a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: a ברייתא already teaches that some people may judge money cases but not capital cases, and רב יהודה said that source includes a ממזר. So why teach it twice?
steps.simpleTranslation: But we already learned this once: anyone fit to judge capital cases is fit to judge money cases, and there is someone fit to judge money cases who is not fit to judge capital cases. And we asked about it: to include whom? And רב יהודה said: to include a ממזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה's answer. The same lesson already comes from a different source, which he himself explained as including a ממזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא already teaches that a ממזר may judge money cases, the 'all' in our משנה seems to repeat it. Each extra word is supposed to teach something new, so the doubling is a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: we already learned it one time

phrases.english: But we already learned this one time:
Anyone who is fit to judge capital cases
is fit to judge money cases,
and there is one who is fit to judge money cases
but is not fit to judge capital cases.
And we discussed it:
To include whom?
phrases.notes: Who is the 'one fit for money cases but not capital cases'?

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:
To include a mamzer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 11 by showing its lesson is already taught elsewhere.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's reading that the משנה's 'all' includes a ממזר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא already includes a ממזר (by רב יהודה's own reading), so the משנה would be repeating it for nothing.

steps.title: One source includes a גר, the other a ממזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two sources teach different things: one includes a גר and the other includes a ממזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: One is to include a convert, and one is to include a ממזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The two sources are not repeating each other, because each one adds a different person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One extra phrase teaches that a גר may judge money cases, and the other teaches the same about a ממזר. So no word is wasted.

phrases.english: One is to include a convert,
and one is to include a mamzer.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא לְאֵתוֹיֵי גֵּר, וַחֲדָא לְאֵתוֹיֵי מַמְזֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the repetition challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources so each teaches a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to teach the same thing about a ממזר.
steps.terutzMaskana: One source includes a גר and the other includes a ממזר, so both are fit to judge money cases.

steps.title: Why both the גר and the ממזר had to be taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that we could not learn one case from the other. A גר may enter the קהל but comes from non-Jewish parents. A ממזר comes from Jewish parents but may not enter the קהל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both are needed. If it taught only a גר, I would say that is because he may marry into the קהל, but a ממזר could not judge. If it taught only a ממזר, I would say that is because he comes from Jewish parents, but a גר, who does not, could not judge. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the answer of step 13 holds up by showing that each case has its own strong point. Neither case can be learned from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person has a different strength and a different weakness. A גר is fully allowed to marry into the Jewish people, while a ממזר is Jewish by birth. Since either strength might be the reason he may judge, both the משנה and the ברייתא were needed, one for each case.

keyTerms.meaning: it is needed (both teachings are necessary)
to enter the congregation (to marry a regular Jew)
a kosher drop (born from Jewish parents)

steps.whatToRemember: Both a גר and a ממזר may judge money cases. Each needs his own source, because each has a strength the other lacks: the גר may enter the קהל, and the ממזר comes from Jewish parents.
steps.confusionAlert: This step does not say a גר or ממזר may judge capital cases. Both are fit only for money cases.

phrases.english: And both are needed,
for if it had taught us only a convert,
[I would say that is] because he is fit to enter the congregation,
phrases.notes: He is allowed to marry a regular Jew, which a ממזר is not.

phrases.english: but a mamzer, I would say no.
And if it had taught us only a mamzer,
[I would say that is] because he comes from a kosher drop,
phrases.notes: He was born to Jewish parents.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל גֵּר דְּלֹא בָּא מִטִּיפָּה כְּשֵׁרָה
phrases.english: but a convert, who does not come from a kosher drop,
I would say no.
Both are needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up step 13 by showing that neither case could have been learned from the other.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both a גר and a ממזר may judge money cases, and each needs its own source because each has a different strength.

steps.title: Why can't everyone judge capital cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that not all may judge דיני נפשות and asks for the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said not everyone is fit to judge capital cases. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second half of the משנה and asks for the source of the rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא explained who is included in 'all are fit' for money cases. Now it asks why capital cases are stricter, so that only people with a clean family line may judge them.

keyTerms.meaning: Capital cases, where a life is at stake

phrases.english: But not all are fit
to judge capital cases.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the money-case half of the משנה to the capital-case half.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason and source for limiting who may judge דיני נפשות.

steps.title: The court must be clean of every flaw
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that just as the בית דין is clean in justice, it must also be clean of every מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: just as the court must be pure in justice, it must also be pure of every flaw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא from רב יוסף: the court must be free of every flaw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here a 'flaw' includes a problem in family line, which explains the משנה's rule. A court judging life and death must be fully clean, not only fair in judgment.

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef taught:
Just as the court is clean in justice,
so too it is clean of every blemish.
phrases.notes: Here 'blemish' includes a flaw in family line, which fits the משנה's rule about who may judge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The בית דין must be free of any מום, including a flawed family line.

steps.title: The verse: 'There is no blemish in you'
steps.stepSummary: אמימר finds the source for רב יוסף's teaching in שיר השירים.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: Which verse teaches this? 'You are all fair, my love, and there is no blemish in you.'
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר gives the פסוק behind רב יוסף's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes the beloved as having 'no blemish' at all. אמימר reads it as a requirement that the court have no flaw at all.

phrases.english: Ameimar said: What is the verse?
'You are all fair, my love,'
and there is no blemish in you.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a פסוק for רב יוסף's ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב יוסף's rule that the court must be free of any מום.

steps.title: Maybe it means a physical defect
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: perhaps the פסוק is talking about a real bodily defect, not family line.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the verse means an actual physical blemish?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof: the word 'blemish' might simply mean a defect in the body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק is about physical defects, it says nothing about family line. Then the משנה's rule about lineage would have no source.

phrases.english: But perhaps it means an actual blemish?
phrases.notes: He means a defect in the body itself, not a problem with the judge's family.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how אמימר's פסוק is read.
steps.kashyaTarget: אמימר's use of שיר השירים as a source for family line.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word מום can simply mean a physical defect, so the פסוק may not teach anything about lineage.

steps.title: Physical defects come from a different verse
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב says physical defects are already learned from 'with you,' so שיר השירים is left to teach about family line.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב said: The verse says, 'That they may stand there with you.' 'With you' means people similar to you.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יעקב answers that we already know physical wholeness from a פסוק about משה's elders.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judges must be 'with you,' meaning like משה, who had no bodily defect. Since physical defects are covered by this פסוק, the שיר השירים פסוק must be teaching something else: a clean family line.

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
The verse says: 'That they may stand there with you'
'with you' means similar to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a separate source for physical defects, which frees the first פסוק for family line.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שיר השירים פסוק might only be about bodily defects.
steps.terutzMaskana: Bodily defects come from 'עמך', so שיר השירים teaches about lineage.

steps.title: Maybe that was only because of the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away רב אחא's proof: משה's elders needed to be whole because the שכינה was going to rest on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps there it was because of the Divine Presence?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from משה's elders.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Those elders were about to receive the שכינה, which may require a whole body. That would not prove anything about ordinary judges, so the source for physical defects is gone again.

phrases.english: But perhaps there it was because of the Divine Presence?
phrases.notes: In that פרשה the elders were about to receive the spirit that rested on משה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source brought in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only רב אחא בר יעקב's פסוק, not the rule itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That case is special because of the שכינה, so it may not apply to regular judges.

steps.title: A better verse: 'They shall bear it with you'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק brings a פסוק about appointing regular judges, which teaches they must be like משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן בר יצחק said: The verse says, 'and they shall bear it with you.' 'With you' means they should be similar to you.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק replaces the rejected proof with a פסוק about ordinary judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק is from יתרו's advice to appoint judges, and the שכינה is not involved there. So it truly teaches that judges must be physically whole. The שיר השירים פסוק then teaches that they also need a clean family line.

keyTerms.meaning: And they shall bear the load with you

steps.whatToRemember: Judges for capital cases must be physically whole (from 'ונשאו אתך') and have a clean family line (from 'ומום אין בך').

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
The verse says: 'And they shall bear it with you'
'with you' means they should be similar to you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer to step 18 after step 20 rejected the first one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new source for physical defects that has nothing to do with the שכינה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without a source for physical defects, the שיר השירים פסוק might be about the body.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'אתך' teaches physical wholeness for regular judges, so שיר השירים teaches family line.

steps.title: The סנהדרין sat in a half circle
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: the סנהדרין sat like half of a round threshing floor so the judges could see each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: The סנהדרין sat like half of a round threshing floor, so that they could all see one another.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and describes how the judges of the סנהדרין were seated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judges sat in a half circle instead of straight rows. This way every judge could see all the others.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
The Sanhedrin was
like half of a round threshing floor,

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּהוּ רוֹאִין זֶה אֶת זֶה.
phrases.english: so that they would see one another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on the layout of the court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The סנהדרין sat in a half circle so all judges could see each other.

steps.title: Two scribes record the judges' opinions
steps.stepSummary: Two scribes stand before the judges, one on each side, and write the opinions for guilty and for innocent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two judges' scribes stand before them, one on the right and one on the left, and write the words of those who find guilty and those who acquit.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and describes the scribes who wrote down what each judge said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scribes write down the opinions of the judges who find the accused liable and of those who acquit him. This is the view of the first תנא, and רבי יהודה will disagree next.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who find the accused liable

phrases.english: And two scribes of the judges
stand before them,
one on the right and one on the left,
and they write the words of those who find liable
and the words of those who acquit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the description of the court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two scribes stand before the court and record the opinions of the judges who find liable and of those who acquit.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: there were three scribes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says there were three scribes: one for acquitting opinions, one for guilty opinions, and a third who writes both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: three. One writes the words of those who acquit, one writes the words of those who find liable, and the third writes both.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion in the משנה about how many scribes there were.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי יהודה's setup, each of the first two scribes writes only one side. The third writes everything, so his record can be checked against the other two.

and the third writes
the words of those who acquit and the words of those who find liable.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: There were three scribes: one for each side, and a third who records both.
